clinicalPearls: Chronic, progressive bacterial infection that predominantly involves the genital region and is regarded as a sexually transmitted infection of low infectivity (Harrison 22e p.1356).
Caused by Klebsiella granulomatis comb nov; the older name Calymmatobacterium granulomatis is still favored by some authorities based on 16S rRNA gene sequence analysis (Harrison 22e p.1356).

Diagnosis is confirmed by microscopic identification of intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies (about 1.5 x 0.7 micrometers) within large mononuclear Pund cells, where they appear as gram-negative cysts with a characteristic safety-pin appearance (Harrison 22e p.1356-1357).

When donovanosis is suspected clinically, the smear for Donovan bodies should be obtained before swabs for other genital ulcer pathogens so adequate material is collected; smears can be read at the bedside with rapid Giemsa or Wright stain (Harrison 22e p.1357).

An experienced clinician's diagnosis based on lesion appearance has a high positive predictive value, and donovanosis is probably the most readily recognizable cause of genital ulceration (Harrison 22e p.1357-1358).

Four lesion types are described: classic beefy-red ulcerogranulomatous ulcer that bleeds easily on touch, hypertrophic/verrucous ulcer with a raised irregular edge, necrotic foul-smelling destructive ulcer, and sclerotic/cicatricial fibrous lesion (Harrison 22e p.1357).
Genitalia are affected in about 90% of patients and the inguinal region in about 10%; lymphadenitis is uncommon, in contrast to other ulcerative STIs (Harrison 22e p.1357).
Cervical lesions can mimic cervical carcinoma, and in men lesions are associated with lack of circumcision (Harrison 22e p.1357).

Extragenital lesions occur in about 6% of cases and may involve the lip, gums, cheek, palate, pharynx, larynx, and chest; hematogenous spread to liver and bone has been reported (Harrison 22e p.1357).

Donovanosis is a recognized risk factor for HIV infection, and its global decline likely reflects more effective management of genital ulcers given their role in HIV transmission (Harrison 22e p.1357).
The estimated incubation period is approximately 50 days based on experimental human infection, though it remains uncertain (Harrison 22e p.1357).

A diagnostic PCR exploits two unique base changes in the phoE gene that eliminate Hae111 restriction sites, distinguishing K. granulomatis from related Klebsiella species; a multiplex genital-ulcer PCR including K. granulomatis exists (Harrison 22e p.1357).
harrison.pathophysiology: Donovanosis is a chronic granulomatous infection caused by the intracellular gram-negative organism Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly Calymmatobacterium granulomatis). The lesion begins as a papule or subcutaneous nodule that ulcerates, often after trauma. The organism resides within macrophages and the stratum malpighii as intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies inside large mononuclear (Pund) cells; these cysts rupture and release infective organisms. Histology shows chronic inflammation with infiltration by plasma cells and neutrophils, and epithelial changes including ulceration, microabscesses, and elongation of the rete ridges. The organism resisted reproducible culture until the mid-1990s, when isolation in peripheral-blood monocytes and human epithelial cell lines was achieved (Harrison 22e p.1356-1357).
additionalDifferentials: Secondary syphilis with condylomata lata (Harrison 22e p.1357)
nonInfectiousMimics: Cervical carcinoma (cervical lesions may mimic it) (Harrison 22e p.1357)
additionalInvestigations: Tissue smear for Donovan bodies stained with rapid Giemsa or Wright stain (Harrison 22e p.1357)
Crush preparation of granulation tissue spread between two slides (Harrison 22e p.1357)
Histologic biopsy showing chronic inflammation, microabscesses, and rete ridge elongation (Harrison 22e p.1357)
phoE gene PCR with colorimetric detection to differentiate K. granulomatis from related Klebsiella species (Harrison 22e p.1357)
Multiplex genital-ulcer PCR including K. granulomatis (Harrison 22e p.1357)
redFlags: Late presentation with extensive ulceration (Harrison 22e p.1357-1358)
Cervical lesion mimicking carcinoma requiring exclusion of malignancy (Harrison 22e p.1357)
Neoplastic change developing within chronic lesions (Harrison 22e p.1357)
Stenosis of the urethra, vagina, or anus (Harrison 22e p.1357)
Lesions in newborns (may present as ear infection) or children, prompting evaluation for source of infection (Harrison 22e p.1357)
harrison.prognosis: Donovanosis is a treatable condition, and reassurance is an important part of care given the embarrassment and low self-esteem many patients experience. It is now confined to a few specific geographic locations, has been almost entirely eliminated in Australia and is close to elimination in South Africa, and its global eradication is considered a distinct possibility. Surgery may be required for very advanced lesions, and patients treated for shorter courses require monitoring until lesions heal completely (Harrison 22e p.1357-1358).
pitfalls: Collecting other genital-ulcer swabs before the Donovan body smear can leave insufficient material for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1357).
Serologic tests are only poorly specific and are not currently used, so they should not be relied upon (Harrison 22e p.1357).
Mixed infections with other genital ulcer pathogens are common and may obscure the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1357).
Lymphadenitis is uncommon, so its absence should not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1357).
Cervical lesions can be mistaken for cervical carcinoma and vice versa (Harrison 22e p.1357).
During pregnancy lesions develop more quickly and respond more slowly, so closer monitoring is needed (Harrison 22e p.1357).
harrison.severityClassification: No formal severity grading is given. Lesions are categorized morphologically into four types: classic ulcerogranulomatous, hypertrophic/verrucous, necrotic/destructive, and sclerotic/cicatricial (Harrison 22e p.1357).
